name: Sāṃkhya
description: Very influential for the other schools of [ShowCultureGroupName('indian_group')] philosophy, $samkhya_school$ is a dualistic school based on rationality. It proposes that the world is composed of both matter and spirit, and that knowledge can only be gained through perception and rational inference.

name: Yoga
description: Similar in many ways to the $samkhya_school$ school, $yoga_school$ also sees the universe as a duality and perception and rationality as ways of gaining knowledge. However, it adds that systematic practice and experimentation are also required to attain knowledge and liberation.

name: Nyāya
description: $nyaya_school$ is a realist school, focusing on methodology and logic as the means of gaining knowledge. It states that our suffering is caused by mistakes due to incorrect knowledge and that liberation will be gained with the correct knowledge.

name: Vaiśeṣika
description: $vaisheshika_school$ is a naturalist, atomistic school, claiming that all physical universe is formed by atoms and that all our experiences come from the aggregations and interactions of such atoms. A complete understanding of the world of experience is thus what brings us to knowledge.

name: Mīmāṃsā
description: The $mimamsa_school$ focuses on the methodology of interpretation and critical explanation of texts. As such, it has a greater focus on philology, the philosophy of languages, and linguistic analysis.

name: Vedānta
description: A very influential and diverse school, $vedanta_school$ focuses on the study of the Vedas, claiming that they are the main source of knowledge, arguing that spiritual matters are beyond any kind of perception and inference by humans.

name: Ibāḍī
description: Believed to be a descendant of the Al-Khawārij, who first were supporters of 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib but later rejected his arbitration. The $ibadi_school$ school distanced itself from the Al-Khawārij following 'Abd Allāh ibn Ibāḍ, taking a more moderate approach and a more positive view towards different $muslim_ADJ$ branches, having similarities with many of the other schools.

name: Mula Sangh
description: Meaning 'root', it refers to the original practices of [ShowReligionName('jain')] coming from Kundakunda, a [ShowReligionAdjectiveWithNoTooltip('jain')] monk from the second century who authored many texts on [ShowReligionAdjectiveWithNoTooltip('jain')] philosophy, and the most important teacher for Digambara [ShowReligionNameWithNoTooltip('jain')].

name: Balatkara Gana
description: A section of [ShowReligiousSchoolName('mula_sangh_school')], the $balatkara_gana_school$ monastic order of [ShowReligionName('jain')] originated in the 8th century with the founder of the $STR_ADJ$ dynasty. As such, it is among the oldest in [ShowReligionNameWithNoTooltip('jain')].

name: Kashtha Sangha
description: A prominent [ShowReligionAdjective('jain')] Digambara monastic school across Northern and Western $india$, originated with Lohacharya, that is, Sudharmāsvāmī. He was the fifth disciple of Mahāvīra, the 24th (and last) of the Tīrthaṅkara.

name: Upkeśa Gaccha
description: The oldest monastic order of Śvetāmbara [ShowReligionName('jain')], it follows the lineage of Pārasanātha, the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara, unlike most other schools that follow the lineage of Mahāvīra.

name: Kharatara Gaccha
description: Also called #italic Vidhisangha#! or #italic Vidhimarga#!, meaning 'the Assembly' and 'Path of Proper Conduct' respectively, it is a Śvetāmbara monastic order that sees its own practices as the only spiritual correct ones. It encourages strict adherence to purity and religious doctrine and scriptures without deviation.

name: Tapa Gaccha
description: Founded by Acharya Jagatchandra Suri, called 'The Meditative One', it is a Śvetāmbara monastic order that encourages veneration of religious figures and pilgrimage to holy temples.

name: Tristutik Gaccha
description: Also known as Agama Gaccha, it is a Śvetāmbara monastic order that focuses on devotion and veneration of the Tīrthaṅkara in its rituals, considering them the only worthy of worship.

name: Ja'farī
description: The $jafari_school$ Madhhab is named after Ja'far al-Ṣādiq, the sixth Imām, and it focuses on independent reasoning by experts of Islamic Law, prefering that over analogy when establishing the Law. It also allows for a temporary marriage lasting a predeterminate period of time.

name: Ismā'īlī
description: The $ismaili_school$ Madhhab is named after Ismā'īl ibn Ja'far, the successor of Ja'far al-Ṣādiq, and was the dominant school of faith in the Fatimid Caliphate but has lost much ground since its fall. The $ismaili_school$ school encompasses a number of increasingly divergent branches, and in many ways, they focus on the esoteric elements of [ShowReligionAdjective('shia')] faith more than the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('jafari_school')] or [ShowReligiousSchoolName('zaidi_school')].

name: Zaydī
description: Also called 'Fivers', the $zaidi_school$ current is named after Zayd ibn 'Alī, the grandson of Muḥammad's son 'Alī, and follows his teachings as described in the Majmu' al-Fiqh. $zaidi_school$ followers emphasize justice and human responsibility and descend from those who supported Zayd's original revolt against the Umayyad Caliph. $zaidi_school$ people entirely reject religious dissimulation as practiced by many [ShowReligionAdjective('shia')] followers, and it is the most similar to [ShowReligionName('sunni')].

name: Imāmīya
description: Also called 'Twelvers', $imamiya_school$ believes that 'Alī, the successor of Muḥammad, was followed by twelve infallible Imām chosen by divine decree. The last Imām, al-Mahdī, is expected to return as the savior of mankind, finally enforcing justice and peace in the world. They mainly follow [ShowReligiousSchoolName('jafari_school')] jurisprudence.

name: Nizārī
description: The $nizari_school$ claim that Nizār ibn al-Mustanṣir was the true successor to the Fatimid Caliphate after his father death, and oppose al-Afḍal Shāhanshāh's coup to install Al-Musta'lī bi'llāh on the throne. Having originally split from the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('ismaili_school')], they have gained adherents from many other branches, and they follow [ShowReligiousSchoolName('jafari_school')] jurisprudence, focusing on pluralism and acceptance of differences.

name: Musta'lī
description: The $mustali_school$ stand in opposition to the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('nizari_school')] in that they accept the ascension of Al-Musta'lī bi'llāh to the throne of the Fatimid Caliphate. Although originating in [ShowRegionName('egypt_region')], they later spread to Western $india$ through missionary work.

name: Alevism
description: Following the teachings of Ḥājī Baktāš Walī, $alevism_school$ is a syncretic mystical school, emerging from the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('imamiya_school')] school but incorporating traditions from [ShowReligionName('tengri')] and older [ShowCultureGroupName('turkic_group')] beliefs. It also takes some aspects of Sufism, like the presence of a spiritual leader and mysticism practices.

name: 'Alawī
description: The $alawi_school$, also called Nuṣairī, proclaim 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the first Imām according to [ShowReligionAdjective('shia')] beliefs, to be the manifestation of $muslim_god_name$ Himself. They differ substantially from the rest of the [ShowReligionAdjective('shia')] faith in both rituals and theology, believing in reincarnation and allowing the consumption of alcohol.

name: Bektashi
description: Named after Ḥājī Baktāš Walī, believed to be descendant of 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the $bektashi_school$ of Sufism nonetheless respects all companions of Muḥammad. Although originating from the [ShowReligionAdjective('sunni')] faith, it contains many beliefs and practices present also in other traditions, giving it many similarity to them.

name: Chishtī
description: Originating from [ShowLocationName('chishti_sarif')], the $chishti_school$ rejects wordly power and promotes tolerance and love. It also promotes music and poetry as a form to connect with the love of $muslim_god_name$.

name: Ḵalwātī
description: The $khalwati_school$ takes its name from the act of retreating oneself for spiritual exercises in solitary. Thus, it emphasizes the individual ritual and spiritual practices, as well as retreat and asceticism.

name: Mevlevi
description: Known for its whirling dervishes, the $mevlevi_school$ is formed upon the teachings of Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Rūmī. It proclaims love as central to [ShowReligionGroupName('muslim')], and it also emphasizes Sema, the movement meditation ceremony performed by way of whirling.

name: Naqshbandī
description: Tracing its origin to Ja'far ibn Muḥammad al-Ṣādiq, the $naqshbandi_school$ places more importance to the $sharia$ than other related schools. Its practices are organized around the silent invocation and conciousness.

name: Qādirī
description: Founded by 'Abdulqādir Gīlānī, the $qadiri_school$ promote a strict following of [ShowReligionAdjective('sunni')] law. It also has decentralized leadership, allowing each of its centers freedom of interpretation and practice, which has caused it to differenciate in multiple branches.

name: Ṣafavī
description: Founded by Ṣāfī ad-Dīn Isḥāq Ardabīlī upon the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('shafii_school')] teachings, the $safavid_school$ has later gotten close to the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('imamiya_school')] thought. Its zeal and strength of belief make its followers be certain of their place in the universe.

name: Shāḏilī
description: Following the teachings of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shāḏilī, the $shadhili_school$ promotes a life of contemplation and to be constantly mindful of $muslim_god_name$, even during normal everyday activities. Applying the teachings of [ShowReligionGroupName('muslim')] to the follower's own lives is the key to transform their existance.

name: Suhrawardī
description: The $suhrawardi_school$ follows the teachings of Abū al-Najīb Abd al-Qādir Suhrawardī, but it is also influenced by the philosophy of Junayd of [ShowLocationName('baghdad')]. It states that people should devote themselves to true knownledge and being faithful to $muslim_god_name$, renouncing natural desires in favor of the spiritual needs.

name: 'Īsāwī
description: Considered the most mystic of the religious schools, the $isawiyya_school$ has its roots from the lands of [ShowRegionName('maghreb_region')] whose heritage of psalms and prayers developed into rituals featuring dance and music.

name: Dīn-i Ilāhī
description: Adopted from the Mongol code, $din_i_ilahi_school$ treats all religions as different sects, allowing the freedom of thought within the realm.

name: Ḥanafī
description: The $hanafi_school$ Madhhab is named after Abū Ḥanīfa Al-Nu'mān ibn Thābit. The school originated in Kufa and is prominent throughout the [ShowCultureName('farsi_culture')] and [ShowCultureGroupName('turkic_group')] world, including northern $india$. Though textual sources in the $common_string_quran$ and Ḥadīth are given preference, $hanafi_school$ followers have an inclusive view of sources and also employ analogy (Qiyās), juristic discretion (Istiḥsan), and local customs ('Urf) in their jurisprudence. Some view it as the most flexible of the schools.

name: Ḥanbalī
description: The $hanbali_school$ Madhhab is named after Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and champions withholding from any speculative theology, Kalām. $hanbali_school$ followers maintain that the $common_string_quran$ and Sunnah are the only proper sources of jurisprudence and that they should be interpreted in a literal and traditionalist sense. Though it is accepted as a valid Madhhab, very few states actively promote the $hanbali_school$ school, and it was banned by the Abbasid Caliphs.

name: Mālikī
description: The $maliki_school$ Madhhab is named after Mālik ibn Anas and is prominent in particular throughout [ShowSubContinentName('north_africa')] and [ShowRegionName('iberia_region')]. Jurisprudence is primarily based on the work and interpretations of ibn Anas and his student Saḥnūn as described in the al-Muwaṭṭa' and the Mudawwanah. One of the foremost centers of learning within the $maliki_school$ School is the Great Mosque of Āl Qayrawān, near [ShowLocationName('tunis')].

name: Shāfi'ī
description: The $shafii_school$ Madhhab is named after Imām Al-Shāfi'ī, and it is prominent in particular among [ShowReligionGroupAdjective('muslim')] believers in [ShowRegionName('arabia_region')], [ShowSubContinentName('east_africa')], and East [ShowContinentName('asia')]. Unlike other Madhhab, the $shafii_school$ reject Istiḥsan and Istislah as sources of $sharia$, instead only relying on what is textually in the $common_string_quran$ or Ḥadīth.

name: Ẓāhirī
description: The $zahiri_school$ advocates for a strict adherence to the text of the $common_string_quran$, and focus on its external or apparent meaning. According to them, there can not be any conclusion drawn from reading the texts that is not in the texts themselves, otherwise $muslim_god_name$ would have explicitly expressed those already.

name: Ash'arī
description: The $ashari_school$ School of Theology is focused on the authority of the scriptures and rationalism, and was founded in the 9th century by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ash'arī. His teachings of all universe being composed of atoms became the basis of the $ashari_school$ School proposition that all matter and time has been created by $muslim_god_name$, believing at the same time in free will and predestination.

name: Māturīdī
description: The $maturidi_school$ School of Theology, taking the name from 'Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī, is a [ShowReligionAdjective('sunni')] school of theology emerging from the theological beliefs of the $hanafi_school$ School of Jurisprudence. It promotes the rational interpretation of the scriptures, and the importance of faith over one person's deeds.

name: Aṯarī
description: The $athari_school$ School of Theology rejects a rational interpretation of the scriptures in favor of a stricter reading of the texts of the $common_string_quran$ and Ḥadīth, considering them the sole authorities. Being against any form of religion innovation, refuses any kind of rationality that is not based upon the texts of the $common_string_quran$.

name: Mu'tazilī
description: The $mutazili_school$ School of Theology developed influenced by Greek and Indian philosophy and rationalism. It rejects the notion that the $common_string_quran$ and $muslim_god_name$ are coexistent, expressing that the scripture must logically come after the originator. It defends reason as long as it serves people to understand religious matters, and it supports that evil originates from errors of humanity due to their free will.

name: Wahhābī
description: Emerging from the [ShowReligiousSchoolName('hanbali_school')] School as a revivalist movement, the $wahhabi_school$ School of Theology is against common Sufi practices like the veneration of holy people and pilgrimages to their shrines. It encourages a return to the original piety and practices of the first generations of [ShowReligionGroupName('muslim')].
